lines.text: Coming up after the break: the hidden chemical in your takeout that could be making you sick!

shots.on_screen: Dark wall of 9 retro TVs (3x3 grid, see continuity TVWALL). Static flickers on all screens; the CENTER TV (B2) switches on: HOST silhouette behind a talk-show desk, pointing at camera. Off-screens keep faint static.
shots.camera: Slow push-in from full wall toward B2 (ends ~70% frame on B2).

lines.text: MSG is an excitotoxin. It overexcites your brain cells. Literally to death.

shots.on_screen: Top-left TV (A1): TV DOCTOR silhouette (white coat, stethoscope shape). Inset on screen: a simple brain icon with jittery zig-zag 'overexcited' lines that fizzle out on 'to death'. No gore, no skulls.
shots.camera: Whip-pan from B2 to A1, then gentle drift right.

lines.text: We never use MSG in my kitchen. Never! It's poison, darling.

shots.on_screen: Top-right TV (C1): CELEBRITY CHEF silhouette (toque), arms crossed, wagging finger. On 'Never!' an MSG shaker on screen gets a big warning-colored X slammed over it.
shots.camera: Whip-pan A1 -> C1; small punch-in (5%) on 'Never!'.

lines.text: Every time I eat Chinese food I get headaches, my heart races... it's the MSG, you guys!

shots.shot_size: MEDIUM (single TV, vertical phone frame inside)
shots.on_screen: Bottom-left TV (A3) shows a vertical phone-video frame: WELLNESS INFLUENCER silhouette with ring-light halo. Pop-up icons: headache (zig-zag at temple), racing heart (pulsing). A PLAIN generic takeout box icon only (no lettering, no pagoda/lantern/chopstick-font cliches).
shots.camera: Whip-pan C1 -> A3 (diagonal); slow drift up.

lines.text: Sharing this for everyone. MSG is basically brain poison! Please read!!

shots.on_screen: Bottom-right TV (C3) shows a social-media post card typing itself out (illegible placeholder lines + shouty caps keyword). Share-arrow icon bounces. Generic UI only - no real platform logo/colors.
shots.camera: Whip-pan A3 -> C3, slow push into the post card.

lines.text: For more than fifty years, three little letters have terrified diners around the world.

shots.on_screen: All five speaker TVs are on simultaneously, looping their keywords; the 4 filler TVs show static. The wall shrinks into a dark room/void as the narrator takes over; the three letters 'MSG' float up big in front.
shots.camera: Fast pull-back from C3 to full wall, then continuous slow pull-back.
shots.notes: Keep DRAMATIZATION tags visible on any TV whose talking head is still readable.

lines.text: Restaurants hang signs promising they don't use it. Food labels proudly brag about leaving it out.

shots.on_screen: Night street: restaurant window. The NO MSG neon sign buzzes on letter by letter (NO, then MSG), stutters once, then holds.
shots.transition_out: Pan right / wipe to supermarket shelf
shots.hero: HERO 1 - first appearance of the NO MSG sign (paid off in s09).

lines.text: Restaurants hang signs promising they don't use it. Food labels proudly brag about leaving it out.

shots.on_screen: Supermarket shelf of generic snack/soup packages; badge stickers stamp onto them one by one (fictional brands only, no real logos).
shots.camera: Lateral truck left->right along the shelf.

lines.text: But what actually is MSG? Is it really bad for you?

shots.on_screen: MSG shaker alone, centered in a spotlight on an empty table, crystals glinting. A large '?' pops above it on 'Is it really bad for you?'.

lines.text: And if it isn't... why does almost everyone think it is?

shots.on_screen: Record scratch: frame freezes for ~0.3 s. Then pull back: the shaker sits small in front of the (now dim) TV wall and the NO MSG sign; a big 'WHY?' rises. Fade out.
shots.camera: Freeze, then smooth pull-back to wide.
shots.hero: HERO 2 - record scratch + 'WHY?' (the video's central question).

lines.text: MSG. The most misunderstood molecule in your kitchen.

shots.on_screen: Starfield; small crystals orbit; the glutamate mascot (face on) pops in at center with a glow (~0.7 s).
shots.camera: Slow linear push-in over whole scene (1.00 -> 1.08).
shots.notes: Already implemented in scenes/s02_title.js - this entry documents it for continuity.

lines.text: MSG. The most misunderstood molecule in your kitchen.

shots.on_screen: Title type rises under the bobbing mascot: 'MSG' (large) then subtitle.
shots.hero: HERO 3 - title card; mascot design is canonical from here on.

lines.text: Our story begins in Tokyo, in 1908.

shots.on_screen: Tokyo, 1908, at dusk: period-accurate wooden two-storey buildings, telegraph poles, lanterns over a street, a lit university-lab window. Respectful, not exoticized (no generic 'Asia' cliches).
shots.camera: Slow descending crane toward the lit window.
shots.transition_out: Push through the window (match to interior)

lines.text: A chemist named Kikunae Ikeda was eating a bowl of soup made with kombu, a kind of seaweed.

shots.on_screen: Interior: Professor Ikeda (period suit, moustache, round glasses - see continuity IKEDA) at a table, blowing on a steaming bowl. A kombu strip floats up out of the bowl as an icon.
shots.camera: Slow push-in from medium to medium-close.

lines.text: He noticed a taste that wasn't sweet, or sour, or salty, or bitter. It was something else. Savory. Meaty. Deep.

shots.on_screen: Four taste icons pop into a ring around Ikeda's head as each word is spoken: SWEET, SOUR, SALTY, BITTER. Each dims/greys out right after it appears ('wasn't...').
shots.notes: Word times are estimates; snap each pop to the spoken word in the WAV.

lines.text: He noticed a taste that wasn't sweet, or sour, or salty, or bitter. It was something else. Savory. Meaty. Deep.

shots.on_screen: A fifth empty slot in the ring glows with a mysterious '?' that pulses; three words drift up in sequence.

lines.text: So he went to his lab, boiled down huge amounts of seaweed, and found the source: a substance called glutamic acid.

shots.on_screen: Lab: a comically huge pile of seaweed tumbles into a giant pot over a burner; it starts boiling.
shots.camera: Tilt down following the falling seaweed.

lines.text: So he went to his lab, boiled down huge amounts of seaweed, and found the source: a substance called glutamic acid.

shots.on_screen: Time-lapse: the pile shrinks, steam rises, the pot boils down to a small dish with just a few glinting crystals.
shots.camera: Push-in from pot to dish (ends close on crystals).

lines.text: He named the taste umami. Roughly: delicious taste.

shots.on_screen: The fifth taste slot fills: big word UMAMI pops in center with glow; the four other taste icons re-appear around it as equals. Small translation line below.
shots.hero: HERO 4 - UMAMI is named (fifth taste completes the ring).

lines.text: To turn it into a seasoning, he paired it with sodium, making a stable, salt-like crystal. Monosodium glutamate.

shots.on_screen: The glutamate mascot (first time in the story) meets a small round sodium ion character; they click together.

lines.text: To turn it into a seasoning, he paired it with sodium, making a stable, salt-like crystal. Monosodium glutamate.

shots.on_screen: The pair tiles into a growing, salt-like crystal lattice. Full name appears with M, S and G highlighted.

lines.text: Within a year, it was on sale.

shots.on_screen: Crystals pour into the MSG shaker (first canonical appearance), which lands on a period shop counter.
shots.notes: Do NOT show a year here: script says only 'within a year'.

lines.text: Here's the thing. Glutamate isn't some strange lab-made chemical.

shots.on_screen: Glutamate mascot center. Behind it a lab flask and beaker pop in; on 'lab-made' they get a big X and slide away; mascot shrugs.

lines.text: It's one of the most common amino acids on Earth, a building block of the proteins in every living thing.

shots.on_screen: Zoom out: the mascot is one bead in a long chain of differently-colored beads (amino acids) that folds into a protein blob.

lines.text: It's one of the most common amino acids on Earth, a building block of the proteins in every living thing.

shots.on_screen: Protein blobs drift into silhouettes of living things: a leaf, a fish, a cell, a person.

lines.text: Ripe tomatoes are full of it. So are mushrooms, soy sauce, and parmesan cheese, one of the richest sources of glutamate there is.

shots.on_screen: Ripe tomato (cut-away) glowing softly with tiny glutamate mascots bobbing inside.

lines.text: Ripe tomatoes are full of it. So are mushrooms, soy sauce, and parmesan cheese, one of the richest sources of glutamate there is.

shots.on_screen: Mushrooms and a soy-sauce bottle pop in, forming a row to the right of the tomato, each with a mini mascot.

lines.text: Ripe tomatoes are full of it. So are mushrooms, soy sauce, and parmesan cheese, one of the richest sources of glutamate there is.

shots.on_screen: Parmesan wedge pops in last and largest, sparkles; it is the only food given an emphasis badge.
shots.notes: No glutamate amounts or ranking between tomato/mushroom/soy - script only says parmesan is one of the richest.

lines.text: Human breast milk contains around ten times more free glutamate than cow's milk. Our very first meal is umami.

shots.on_screen: Two simple milk icons side by side: HUMAN MILK (droplet/bottle) and COW'S MILK (glass). Bars rise beneath them: the human-milk bar grows to ~10x the cow's-milk bar.
shots.camera: Locked; slight tilt up following the tall bar.
shots.notes: Bar ratio must be ~10:1. No axis values. Icon-level depiction only (no nudity / breastfeeding scene).

lines.text: Human breast milk contains around ten times more free glutamate than cow's milk. Our very first meal is umami.

shots.on_screen: Swaddled baby smiles with a warm umami glow; a tiny mascot floats by.

lines.text: Your body even makes its own glutamate, every single day.

shots.on_screen: Simple human silhouette with glowing interior; little 'cell factories' produce mascots. A sun/moon arc cycles overhead twice to say 'every day'.

lines.text: And to your body, glutamate from a tomato and glutamate from a shaker of MSG are exactly the same molecule.

shots.on_screen: Left half: tomato releases a glutamate mascot. Right half: MSG shaker shakes out a glutamate mascot.
shots.camera: Locked split; both halves drift slightly.

lines.text: And to your body, glutamate from a tomato and glutamate from a shaker of MSG are exactly the same molecule.

shots.on_screen: Split line dissolves; both mascots slide to center and overlap perfectly (pixel-identical). Big '=' between then over them.
shots.hero: HERO 5 - tomato glutamate = MSG glutamate (the two mascots must be IDENTICAL).

scenes.title: What Happens When You Eat It

lines.text: So what happens when you eat it?

shots.on_screen: A fork lifts a bite of seasoned food from a plate toward a mouth (profile).

lines.text: First, glutamate docks onto special receptors on your tongue, and sends your brain a message: this food has protein in it. Yum.

shots.on_screen: Cutaway body (side profile head + torso, see BODY). Push into the tongue: taste receptors as little docking cups; glutamate mascots dock with a click and the receptor glows.

lines.text: First, glutamate docks onto special receptors on your tongue, and sends your brain a message: this food has protein in it. Yum.

shots.on_screen: A glowing signal pulse travels up a nerve to the brain; the brain pops a speech bubble.

lines.text: Then it reaches your gut. And this is where the scary story starts to fall apart.

shots.on_screen: Camera dives down the esophagus into the gut tunnel. On 'scary story starts to fall apart' a small '!' alarm bubble (TV-wall style from s01) cracks and crumbles.

lines.text: The cells lining your intestines love glutamate. They burn it as fuel.

shots.on_screen: Intestine-wall close-up: round gut-cell characters (see GUTCELL) gobble passing glutamate mascots and light up with a small energy spark.
shots.hero: HERO 6 - gut cells eat glutamate as fuel (character sheet reused in s06).

lines.text: Almost all the glutamate you eat, around ninety-five percent, is used up right there in your gut, before it ever reaches your bloodstream.

shots.on_screen: A stream of glutamate particles enters; most are eaten. A percentage counter climbs and lands on 95% exactly as 'ninety-five percent' is spoken.
shots.notes: Counter landing time (~24.5 s) is an estimate - snap to the spoken 'ninety-five' in the WAV.

lines.text: Almost all the glutamate you eat, around ninety-five percent, is used up right there in your gut, before it ever reaches your bloodstream.

shots.on_screen: Pull back: gut wall as a border; only a few stray particles slip through into a blood vessel beyond.
shots.notes: Do not print '5%' - only 95% is stated.

lines.text: And the little that slips through faces another wall: the blood-brain barrier, a tightly guarded border that controls what gets into your brain.

shots.on_screen: Follow the few particles up a vessel to the head. A castle-wall barrier rises, with cute guard characters.

lines.text: And the little that slips through faces another wall: the blood-brain barrier, a tightly guarded border that controls what gets into your brain.

shots.on_screen: At the gate a guard checks arrivals; a glutamate particle approaches, the guard raises a palm, it bounces back.

lines.text: The glutamate on your dinner plate doesn't just stroll into your neurons.

shots.on_screen: Full stack: dinner plate at bottom, gut, wall, brain with calm glowing neurons at top. Mascot at the gate shrugs.

lines.text: So how did a seaweed seasoning become public enemy number one?

shots.on_screen: A kombu strip morphs into the MSG shaker; spotlight snaps on and a target-reticle frames it.

lines.text: It started in 1968, with a letter.

shots.on_screen: Chapter label 1968. A typewritten letter flutters down onto a desk.

lines.text: A doctor wrote to the New England Journal of Medicine, describing numbness, weakness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States.

shots.on_screen: Letter close-up: lines type themselves (illegible placeholder text); envelope addressed to the journal.
text: TO: NEW ENGLAND JOURNAL OF MEDICINE
shots.notes: Plain text address only - do not recreate the journal's real masthead/logo.

lines.text: A doctor wrote to the New England Journal of Medicine, describing numbness, weakness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States.

shots.on_screen: Three symptom icons pop out of the letter: tingling hand (numbness), drooping arm (weakness), fluttering heart (palpitations). Beside them a small, NEUTRAL restaurant-front icon with a US flag pin.
shots.notes: No stereotyped restaurant/people imagery (see guardrails).

lines.text: He wondered what might be causing it. The cooking wine? The salt? Maybe the MSG? He didn't know. It was a guess.

shots.on_screen: Suspect line-up: cooking-wine bottle, salt shaker, MSG shaker. A '?' pops above each as it is named.

lines.text: He wondered what might be causing it. The cooking wine? The salt? Maybe the MSG? He didn't know. It was a guess.

shots.on_screen: The three '?' drift together and merge into one wobbly label; the letter-writer (a simple shrugging hand/silhouette, not a portrait) shrugs.

lines.text: But the journal printed it under a catchy headline: Chinese Restaurant Syndrome.

shots.on_screen: The printed headline stamp slams across the letter/page with a camera shake.
shots.camera: Whip-in, then 6-frame shake on impact, then hold.
shots.notes: Stamp lands on the spoken name (~29.3 s, verify). Plain neutral typeface - never a 'chop-suey'/wonton font.

lines.text: Letters poured in. Newspapers ran with it. Almost overnight, a guess had become a diagnosis.

shots.on_screen: Envelopes pour in from the top; newspapers multiply and spin toward camera (classic spinning-paper gag).

lines.text: Letters poured in. Newspapers ran with it. Almost overnight, a guess had become a diagnosis.

shots.on_screen: The 'A GUESS' label morphs into a clipboard-style 'DIAGNOSIS' stamp.

lines.text: A year later, a scientist injected huge doses of MSG under the skin of newborn mice, and found brain damage. The headlines got even scarier.

shots.on_screen: Chapter label 1969. A cute lab with newborn mouse pups in a nest; a comically GIANT syringe looms in (scale gag = huge dose). The injection is implied, never shown; no gore.

lines.text: A year later, a scientist injected huge doses of MSG under the skin of newborn mice, and found brain damage. The headlines got even scarier.

shots.on_screen: Newspapers return with bigger, scarier headlines (illegible except 'MSG' and '!'); a muted alarm bell shakes.

lines.text: But injecting a massive dose into a baby mouse is nothing like eating a seasoned meal. Remember: your gut eats almost all of it first.

shots.on_screen: Left: giant syringe over a tiny mouse pup ('injection'). Right: a person enjoying a seasoned bowl ('meal'). A big not-equal sign between.

lines.text: But injecting a massive dose into a baby mouse is nothing like eating a seasoned meal. Remember: your gut eats almost all of it first.

shots.on_screen: Callback: the s05 gut cells gobble glutamate mascots; the 95% badge from s05 reappears small.
shots.notes: Must reuse GUTCELL and 95% badge exactly as designed in s05.

lines.text: And there was something else going on. In 1960s America, Chinese food was seen as foreign and suspicious.

shots.on_screen: Mood shift (slightly muted palette, still the house style): a 1960s American street with a varied crowd of ordinary diners walking past a NEUTRAL restaurant facade.
shots.notes: Highest-sensitivity shot - see guardrails (no stereotypes, no caricatured Asian people).

lines.text: And there was something else going on. In 1960s America, Chinese food was seen as foreign and suspicious.

shots.on_screen: Suspicion shown abstractly: cold side-eye glances and gray tag-labels drift onto a plain takeout box (the prejudice is visualized as something put ON the food, not as a trait of people).
shots.notes: Words shown in quotes / as tags so they read as the attitude being criticised.

lines.text: Nobody blamed the tomato sauce. Nobody worried about Italian Restaurant Syndrome. The fear stuck to one cuisine, and the name said it out loud.

shots.on_screen: Left: pasta with tomato sauce and parmesan - calm, nothing happens. Right: the takeout box - alarm bells ring. Identical glutamate mascots bob above BOTH sides. A fake headline 'ITALIAN RESTAURANT SYNDROME' fades in on the left and dissolves away (it never existed).

lines.text: Nobody blamed the tomato sauce. Nobody worried about Italian Restaurant Syndrome. The fear stuck to one cuisine, and the name said it out loud.

shots.on_screen: Split collapses onto the right; the original HEADLINE card from shot 07 slides back in; camera pushes in on the name; hold, then fade.
shots.notes: Same HEADLINE card as shot 07, identical typography.

lines.text: Scientists took the claims seriously, and tested them. Again, and again.

shots.on_screen: Clean modern lab, a diverse team of scientists. Clipboards and study folders stack up, each getting a check as 'again, and again' is said.
shots.notes: No study count is given in the script - do not number the folders.

lines.text: The gold standard is a double-blind study: people get either MSG or a placebo, and nobody, not even the researchers, knows who got which.

shots.on_screen: A small gold-standard badge, then two identical capsules labeled A and B on a tray.

lines.text: The gold standard is a double-blind study: people get either MSG or a placebo, and nobody, not even the researchers, knows who got which.

shots.on_screen: Capsules drop under two cups and get shuffled (shell-game). Volunteer AND researcher both wear cute blindfolds - nobody knows which is which.

lines.text: Over and over, people who said they were sensitive to MSG reacted just as often to the fake.

shots.on_screen: A row of diverse volunteers wearing 'SENSITIVE' badges, thought bubbles with worried symptom icons; each takes a cup.

lines.text: Over and over, people who said they were sensitive to MSG reacted just as often to the fake.

shots.on_screen: Results chart: two bars, MSG vs PLACEBO, rise to nearly the same height. Volunteers' reaction icons split evenly between the two groups.
shots.hero: HERO 12 - MSG vs placebo bars nearly equal.
shots.notes: No axis numbers / percentages - the script gives none.

lines.text: Huge doses on an empty stomach caused mild, short-lived symptoms in some people. But the results weren't consistent, and nothing like that showed up with normal amounts in normal food.

shots.on_screen: Comically huge spoonful next to an empty plate/stomach icon; SOME volunteers get small symptom icons that fade away quickly (a short timer runs out).

lines.text: Huge doses on an empty stomach caused mild, short-lived symptoms in some people. But the results weren't consistent, and nothing like that showed up with normal amounts in normal food.

shots.on_screen: Result cards scatter with mixed, inconsistent marks; then they clear and a normal meal plate appears with a relaxed volunteer and a calm check mark.
shots.camera: Pull-back then push-in on the plate.

lines.text: Today, the US Food and Drug Administration lists MSG as generally recognized as safe, the same category as salt, sugar, and baking powder.

shots.on_screen: Official-looking (generic, not a real seal/logo) document slides in; a big GRAS stamp slams onto it.
shots.notes: Stamp on 'generally recognized as safe' (~39.0 s, verify). Plain-text 'US FDA' only; no agency logo.

lines.text: Today, the US Food and Drug Administration lists MSG as generally recognized as safe, the same category as salt, sugar, and baking powder.

shots.on_screen: The MSG shaker joins a row with a salt shaker, a sugar bowl and a baking-powder tin under the GRAS label.

lines.text: Here's a plot twist. MSG might actually help.

shots.on_screen: Swirl/twist transition; MSG shaker in spotlight with a curling twist-arrow and a small heart-shaped spark.

lines.text: Gram for gram, it has only about a third of the sodium of table salt.

shots.on_screen: Balance scale; SALT shaker lands on the left pan, MSG shaker on the right ('gram for gram' - equal weights).
shots.notes: Scale stays level: equal mass is the premise.

lines.text: Gram for gram, it has only about a third of the sodium of table salt.

shots.on_screen: Sodium ions (same Na character as s03) pop out above each shaker: three under SALT, one under MSG.
shots.hero: HERO 14 - about a third of the sodium (3:1 ions).

lines.text: Swap some of the salt in a recipe for MSG, and you can cut the sodium in a dish noticeably, while keeping all the flavor.

shots.on_screen: A cooking pot; a salt spoon is partly swapped for an MSG spoon; a SODIUM meter beside the pot drops.
shots.notes: No specific % reduction - script only says 'noticeably'.

lines.text: Swap some of the salt in a recipe for MSG, and you can cut the sodium in a dish noticeably, while keeping all the flavor.

shots.on_screen: A FLAVOR meter next to the sodium meter stays full; a heart icon pops up and smiles.
shots.notes: Heart is a mood icon; no 'heart health' text or claim.

scenes.title: So... Is MSG Bad for You?

lines.text: So, is MSG bad for you?

shots.on_screen: Callback: the exact s01 TV wall, all five talking heads frozen mid-claim (DRAMATIZATION tags visible); MSG shaker in front with a '?'.

lines.text: In absurd amounts, almost anything is. Even water. But in food, the evidence says it's about as dangerous as the tomato on your pizza.

shots.on_screen: Absurd-dose gag: a comically gigantic water tank next to a normal glass of water.

lines.text: In absurd amounts, almost anything is. Even water. But in food, the evidence says it's about as dangerous as the tomato on your pizza.

shots.on_screen: Balance scale: a pizza slice with tomato on one side, a pinch of MSG on the other - level.

lines.text: The story of MSG is really a story about how one guess, a catchy name, and a little bit of prejudice can outlive decades of science.

shots.on_screen: Three tags tumble in as each phrase is spoken: A GUESS (shape from s06), A CATCHY NAME (HEADLINE card mini), A LITTLE PREJUDICE.
shots.notes: Word times estimated; snap to WAV.

lines.text: The story of MSG is really a story about how one guess, a catchy name, and a little bit of prejudice can outlive decades of science.

shots.on_screen: Pull back to the TV wall: on 'outlive decades of science' the TVs switch off one by one (reverse of s01 order: C3, A3, C1, A1, B2) while a tall stack of research papers rises beside them.

lines.text: So the next time you see a No MSG sign, you'll know the real story.

shots.on_screen: The same NO MSG neon sign from s01; it flickers and the 'NO' burns out, leaving 'MSG' glowing warmly.
shots.hero: HERO 16 - 'NO' burns out (payoff of s01 shot 07).

lines.text: And maybe... you'll reach for the shaker.

shots.on_screen: Cozy steaming bowl of ramen; a hand reaches for the MSG shaker and gives it two shakes.

continuity.name: Glutamate mascot
continuity.rules: Always drawn with KZ.glutamate(ctx,x,y,t,{face:true}) — same atom layout, same face, same proportions as s02. Swarms/particles may use small simplified versions but must read as the same molecule. Never redesign per scene; never give it a menacing face (it is the friendly hero). In s04.11 the two copies must be pixel-identical.
continuity.appears_in: s02, s03.08–09, s04 (most shots), s05 (tongue, gut, barrier), s06.13, s06.16, s09.08

continuity.name: MSG shaker
continuity.rules: Always KZ.shaker(ctx,x,y,s,'MSG') with the same body/cap colors in every scene. Label reads exactly 'MSG'. Same height ratio relative to the SALT shaker whenever both appear. Negative scenes (s01, s06.01) change the lighting/overlays (X, reticle), never the prop itself.

continuity.name: Salt shaker
continuity.rules: KZ.shaker(...,'SALT') — a visibly different body or cap tone than MSG, otherwise identical silhouette (fair comparison). Reused unchanged in s06.05, s07.09, s08.

continuity.name: Retro TV wall
continuity.rules: 3x3 grid of rounded retro TVs, fixed layout reused verbatim in s09. Speaker positions: HOST=B2 (center), TVDOC=A1 (top-left), CHEF=C1 (top-right), GURU=A3 (bottom-left), AUNT=C3 (bottom-right); the 4 remaining TVs show static only. Lighting order in s01: B2, A1, C1, A3, C3. Switch-off order in s09: C3, A3, C1, A1, B2. Talking heads are flat silhouettes with role props (desk, coat, toque, ring light, post card) — no facial likeness to any real person. Build once and share (see PRODUCTION_PLAN.md).

continuity.name: DRAMATIZATION tag
continuity.rules: Small pill tag reading 'DRAMATIZATION' in the same corner of every TV screen whenever a talking head is visible, legible at 1080p (cap height >= 22 px), present for the entire time the head is on screen.
continuity.appears_in: s01.01–06, s09.01 (and any other frame showing a talking head)

continuity.name: NO MSG neon sign
continuity.rules: One design: two words on one line, 'NO' and 'MSG' as separate neon tubes so 'NO' can burn out alone in s09. Same window/frame, same camera angle in both appearances (s09.06 should feel like a return to s01.07).

continuity.name: Gut cells
continuity.rules: Round intestine-cell characters with dot eyes, sitting in a row along the gut wall; gobble animation (mouth opens, mascot vanishes, small energy spark). s06.13 is a callback and must reuse the s05 design, motion and the same '95%' badge styling.

continuity.name: Sodium ion
continuity.rules: Small round 'Na' character (no face or tiny face), identical in s03 (pairing with glutamate) and s08 (counting sodium). In s08 the count is exactly 3 (salt) : 1 (MSG).

continuity.name: Tomato

allowed_numbers_and_claims: 1908, Tokyo, Kikunae Ikeda, kombu, glutamic acid, 'umami ~ delicious taste', sodium + glutamate = monosodium glutamate, on sale 'within a year' (s03) — NO explicit year for the sale
Glutamate: one of the most common amino acids; building block of proteins; in tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, parmesan ('one of the richest sources') (s04)
Human breast milk ~10x more FREE glutamate than cow's milk (s04) — show '~10x', bars ~10:1
Body makes its own glutamate every day; tomato glutamate = MSG glutamate (s04)
~95% of dietary glutamate used up in the gut (s05) — the ONLY percentage in the film; do not show '5%'
1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine; symptoms numbness, weakness, palpitations; suspects wine, salt, MSG; 'a guess'; printed under the headline 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' (s06)
1969 (a year later): huge doses injected under the skin of newborn mice, brain damage found (s06) — no gore

Double-blind placebo-controlled testing; MSG-sensitive people reacted as often to placebo; huge doses on an empty stomach -> mild, short-lived symptoms in some people, inconsistent; nothing with normal amounts in normal food (s07)
US FDA: 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS), same category as salt, sugar, baking powder (s07)
MSG has ~1/3 the sodium of table salt gram for gram; swapping some salt cuts sodium 'noticeably' while keeping flavor (s08) — no % reduction
'In absurd amounts almost anything is [bad], even water'; 'about as dangerous as the tomato on your pizza' (s09)
forbidden: Any number, percentage, chart value, axis label, study count, dose amount or date not listed above (e.g. no '1909', no 'mg/kg', no 'n=...', no glutamate content per food).
Health claims beyond the script: no 'heart healthy', 'cures', 'MSG makes you healthier', 'zero side effects'.
Real logos, mastheads or seals (NEJM, FDA, social platforms, TV networks, food brands). Plain text names only.
Real or recognisable people (celebrity look-alikes, real TV doctors/chefs). The cold-open talking heads are fictional composites.
Showing Olney or Kwok as portraits — use hands/silhouettes or objects (letter, lab).
Gore: no needles piercing animals, no dead mice, no brain lesions imagery.
guardrails.dramatization: Every frame that shows a cold-open talking head (s01.01–06, s09.01, s09.05 if heads still visible) must carry the 'DRAMATIZATION' tag on that screen. Role chyrons use generic labels only: TALK SHOW HOST, DAYTIME TV DOCTOR, CELEBRITY CHEF, WELLNESS INFLUENCER, YOUR AUNT, ON SOCIAL MEDIA.
sensitive_1960s_section: Applies to s01.04 (takeout mention), s06.04, s06.07, s06.11, s06.14–17 and s09.04.
No caricatured Asian people: no slanted-eye shorthand, buck teeth, conical hats, queues, 'coolie' imagery.
No 'oriental' signifiers as shorthand: no wonton/chop-suey fonts, pagoda roofs, gongs, dragons, paper-lantern clusters, chopsticks-in-hair.
Restaurant = neutral storefront; food = plain takeout box / bowl. Crowds are varied ordinary diners.
The prejudice is the subject being criticised: show it as cold tags/glances put ON the food, and frame 'foreign'/'suspicious' in quotes; it should never look endorsed.
The headline text is shown verbatim as a historical artifact in quotation marks; it is not used as a joke or punchline.
Ikeda / Tokyo 1908 (s03) depicted respectfully and period-plausibly, not exoticized.
